result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.subgraph_centrality()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Calculate subgraph centrality scores for all nodes. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L40145-L40203){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.subgraph_centrality( attr_name=None, return_dict=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Subgraph centrality](/assets/graphs/subgraph-centrality.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The shared seven-node strip of triangles with a tail, shaded by subgraph centrality, which counts closed walks that start and end at each node. Hub C sits in three triangles and scores 6.17, ahead of D 4.74 and B 4.67, while the tail nodes F 2.32 and G 1.59, in no triangle, score least." width="100%"} Subgraph centrality (Estrada & Rodríguez-Velázquez, 2005) counts the closed walks that start and end at a node, weighting a walk of length `k` by `1/k!`. Short closed walks (triangles, squares, back-and-forth steps) dominate, so the score rewards nodes that sit inside many small, tightly knit structures rather than simply having many neighbors. Mathematically it is the node's diagonal entry of `exp(A)`, the exponential of the adjacency matrix; summing it over all nodes gives `get_estrada_index()`. It is used in biology (proteins in dense functional modules score high) and to tell apart nodes that a degree count would tie. Edges are treated as unweighted and parallel edges count once. Undirected graphs only. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the node attribute to store scores in. If `None` (default), uses `"subgraph_centrality"`. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, returns a dictionary instead of self. If `False` (default), stores the scores as a node attribute and returns self for chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[dict[int, float], Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: a dictionary mapping node IDs to scores (each at least `1`, from the empty walk). If `return_dict=` is `False` (default): returns self. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} In a triangle with a tail, the triangle's nodes sit on more short closed walks than the tail, even where degrees tie: ::: {#d3a69b6e .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E")]) ) scores = graph.subgraph_centrality(return_dict=True) {graph.get_label_from_id(n): round(s, 3) for n, s in sorted(scores.items())} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'A': 2.785, 'B': 2.785, 'C': 3.545, 'D': 2.303, 'E': 1.593} ``` ::: :::
